newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan excludes early polls in army row.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan excludes early polls in army row.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Saturday ruled out early elections as a solution to his dispute with the secularist army over Islamist activism, Anatolian news agency said.
"Going to elections would mean coming under the influence of a false agenda," the agency quoted Erbakan as telling a meeting of local heads of his Welfare Party.

The prime minister last weekend threatened the divided opposition with snap polls in what was seen as a tactical move. The other parties have not taken up his challenge to ask the voters to mediate his row with the generals.
"There is no alternative to today's government and no other solution," he said on Saturday.

The secularist army has put Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, under heavy pressure to crack down on a Moslem religious upsurge. The generals say curtailing growing Islamist sentiment is a matter of life or death for NATO-member Turkey.
But Erbakan's wing of the coalition government has stalled in taking anti-Islamist action.

Interior Minister Meral Aksener, from the ruling alliance's secularist True Path Party faction, on Saturday vowed to close down thousands of outlawed Islamic education centres in line with army demands.
"Not one illegal Koranic course, religious hostel or similar institution will remain," Anatolian quoted minister her as saying.
"We will take all the necessary precautions to prevent our country's bright horizon from darkening."
Two True Path ministers resigned last weekend but there has been little sign of a much-vaunted anti-Islamist rebellion in the ranks of the party led by Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller.
Ciller said on Thursday her party would not abandon its Islamist coalition partners.
Analysts say MPs of all political hues oppose early elections in fear of losing their seats.
Aksener said the dozens of underground Koranic classes closed by police in recent raids represented less than two percent of the number of illegal courses.
